pages.title: Explorer 1: the Van Allen belts
pages.summary: America’s first satellite carried a Geiger counter that found belts of radiation.

facts.label: Launched
facts.value: 31 January 1958, 10:48 p.m. EST, Cape Canaveral (1 February UT)

facts.label: Orbit
facts.value: About 360 to 2,500 km above the Earth

facts.label: Last signal
facts.value: 23 May 1958, when its batteries ran down

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: US Army (ABMA) and JPL; NASA opened on 1 October 1958

firsts: First US satellite
First US scientific discovery in space
First tape recorder flown on a satellite (Explorer 3)

sections.heading: The flight
sections.text: Sputnik 1 went up on 4 October 1957, and on 6 December the Navy’s Vanguard rocket exploded on its pad. The Army’s team got its chance. Wernher von Braun’s group at the Army Ballistic Missile Agency turned its Jupiter-C into the Juno launcher, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory built the satellite, and the work took 84 days. Explorer 1 left Cape Canaveral at 10:48 p.m. on 31 January 1958, into an orbit somewhat higher than planned. At 1 a.m. William Pickering, James Van Allen and von Braun announced it in Washington, holding a full-size model over their heads.

sections.heading: A counter that went quiet
sections.text: Van Allen, a physicist at the University of Iowa, had built the main instrument: a Geiger counter meant to measure cosmic rays. Explorer 1 carried no tape recorder, so its counts arrived only while it passed near a ground station, a few minutes at a time. Low in the orbit the rate looked as expected. Higher up the counter fell silent. Van Allen came to a surprising reading of this: the tube was not seeing too little radiation but far too much, swamped by charged particles, mainly from the Sun, held in place by the Earth’s magnetic field.

sections.heading: Explorers 3 and 4
sections.text: Explorer 2 failed at launch, but Explorer 3 reached orbit on 26 March 1958 with a small tape recorder built in Van Allen’s department, the first flown on a satellite. Its record showed the count climbing with height to the top of the scale and then dropping to zero, the same pattern laboratory counters gave under very intense radiation. Explorer 4 followed on 26 July with four detectors, some of them shielded, built to measure the belts and the high-altitude nuclear tests of Project Argus. With Pioneer 3’s data that December, a second, outer belt emerged.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Space close to the Earth was not empty. The inner belt, mostly protons, and the outer belt, mostly electrons, were named after Van Allen, and their danger was known before anyone flew in space. In NASA’s own summary, the simple answer was to orbit below the belts, under about 300 nautical miles (some 560 km), and to cross them quickly on the way out. The belts dip lower over the South Atlantic, so the tilt of an orbit set how often a crew passed through that patch. Apollo’s crews crossed the belts on the way to the Moon, and their radiation doses stayed small.

pages.title: Luna 3: the far side of the Moon
pages.summary: The first look at the side of the Moon that never faces the Earth.
firsts: First pictures of the Moon’s far side
First spacecraft to fly past the Moon

sections.heading: The flight
sections.text: Luna 3 left Baikonur on 4 October 1959, two years to the day after Sputnik. The Soviet press called it the Automatic Interplanetary Station; the name Luna 3 came later. It was not aimed at the Moon itself but at a long loop around the Earth that swung it past the Moon’s south pole on 6 October and then up and behind it. Seen from there, the far side was in full sunlight, and the probe’s orbit would bring it back toward Earth to send what it saw.

sections.heading: The pictures
sections.text: On 7 October 1959, with the Moon filling its view, Luna 3 took 29 photographs in about 40 minutes. They covered roughly 70 percent of the far side. The images that reached Earth were faint and full of noise, and only 17 were usable, but they showed something nobody expected: hardly any of the dark, smooth plains that mark the near side. The far side was rough, bright and crowded with craters. Two dark patches stood out, later named Mare Moscoviense and the crater Tsiolkovskiy.

sections.heading: A darkroom in space
sections.text: Television cameras were not yet good enough, so Luna 3 carried a twin-lens film camera with its own darkroom. After the last exposure the film was developed, fixed and dried on board, then scanned by a fine beam of light and sent home line by line as a radio signal, like a fax. The film itself had a strange past: it came from American reconnaissance balloons that had drifted over the Soviet Union, whose unexposed rolls turned out to stand heat and radiation well.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: For all of human history half of the Moon had been out of sight. Luna 3 settled what was there in a single morning, and its pictures went around the world as proof of how far ahead the Soviet program was. Scientists had to explain why the two halves of the Moon are so different, a question that is still studied. A Soviet atlas of the far side followed in 1960, and the names chosen then, for Soviet places and for scientists and writers, are still on the map.

pages.title: Korabl-Sputnik 2: Belka and Strelka come home
pages.summary: The first animals to orbit the Earth and come back alive, in a test Vostok.

facts.label: Craft
facts.value: Korabl-Sputnik 2 (Sputnik 5 in the West), an uncrewed Vostok

facts.label: Launch vehicle
facts.value: 8K72, an R-7 with an upper stage

facts.label: Landed
facts.value: 20 August 1960, near Orsk, after about 26 hours

facts.label: Crew
facts.value: None; the dogs Belka and Strelka, 40 mice, two rats, insects and plants

firsts: First living things brought back alive from orbit

sections.heading: Laika’s one-way trip
sections.text: The first animal in orbit had flown three years earlier. On 3 November 1957 Sputnik 2 carried the dog Laika, a calm stray of about 6 kg, in a padded, sealed cabin with air regeneration, food in jelly form, sensors for her pulse and breathing, and a television camera. Nobody yet knew how to bring a payload back from orbit, so her flight could only end one way. The cabin overheated soon after launch, and Laika died of the heat within days; the sources disagree on exactly when. She still gave doctors their first readings from a living animal in orbit.

sections.heading: The second try
sections.text: Korabl-Sputnik 2 was an uncrewed test model of Vostok, the ship meant to carry the first cosmonaut. A first attempt with the dogs Chayka and Lisichka ended on 28 July 1960 when the rocket broke apart seconds after launch, killing both. On 19 August 1960 the next ship reached an orbit of 306 by 339 km with Belka and Strelka aboard. They rode with 40 mice, two rats, insects, plants, fungi, seeds, microbes and strips of human skin. Two cameras let doctors watch the dogs, and the ship also carried instruments for cosmic rays and ultraviolet and X-ray light.

sections.heading: Watched from the ground
sections.text: The first pictures worried the doctors. At first the dogs lay so still that only the telemetry showed they were alive. Later they moved, but in jerks, and on the fourth orbit Belka struggled and vomited. The ship’s infrared orientation system failed, so engineers turned to the backup that used the Sun, and on the 18th orbit the descent capsule came down at the right angle. The dogs’ cabin was ejected and landed by parachute near Orsk, about 26 hours after launch. Belka and Strelka were in good health. An American Discoverer capsule had come back from orbit nine days earlier, but it carried no one.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: The flight checked almost every main part of the Vostok design, from life support and reentry to the ejection seat the dogs’ cabin rode in, and showed that animals could live through a day in weightlessness and come home. It also left doubts. After seeing Belka on the screen, the head of the medical team, Vladimir Yazdovskiy, told the State Commission that the first cosmonaut should fly only one orbit. The last two test ships, in March 1961, each made a single orbit with a dog and a dummy. On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin flew one orbit in Vostok 1. Strelka later had puppies, and Khrushchev gave one, Pushinka, to Caroline Kennedy.

pages.title: Ranger 7: the Moon up close
pages.summary: After six failures, a probe that filmed the Moon until the moment it hit.

facts.label: Pictures
facts.value: More than 4,300 in the last 17 minutes

firsts: First pictures of the Moon taken by a US spacecraft
First close-up pictures of the lunar surface

sections.heading: The flight
sections.text: Ranger 7 left Cape Kennedy on an Atlas-Agena B on 28 July 1964. Its job was simple to state: fly straight into the Moon and send back television pictures all the way down. After one course correction on 29 July it arrived precisely on target two days later. On 31 July 1964 it struck a plain between Mare Nubium and Oceanus Procellarum at about 2.6 kilometers per second. The spot was later named Mare Cognitum, the Known Sea, as the first place on the Moon seen up close.

sections.heading: The pictures
sections.text: About 17 minutes before impact, at an altitude of some 2,100 kilometers, the first picture came in. Six television cameras then sent more than 4,300 images to the Goldstone station in California, each one closer than the last. The final frames were taken less than a second before impact and were cut off when the spacecraft hit. They showed craters inside craters, down to pits about half a meter across, even on plains that looked smooth from Earth. In many places the detail was a thousand times finer than any telescope could give.

sections.heading: Six failures first
sections.text: Ranger 7 came after a hard run. Rangers 1 and 2 never left Earth orbit. Ranger 3 missed the Moon by tens of thousands of kilometers, Ranger 4 hit the far side with its computer dead, and Ranger 5 missed after a power failure. Ranger 6 reached its target in January 1964 but a short circuit had disabled its cameras, and it returned no pictures at all. The program came under heavy criticism, and its future depended on the next flight.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Before Ranger 7 no one could rule out a Moon too rough, or too deep in dust, for a landing. Its pictures showed a surface battered by impacts at every scale but with level ground in the maria, and scientists concluded that a crewed landing there was possible. Rangers 8 and 9 followed in 1965, then the Surveyor landers. Ranger 7 also ended a long losing streak for American lunar probes, and the successes that followed made it a turning point for the whole program.

pages.title: Pegasus: wings to catch meteoroids
pages.summary: Three winged satellites counted the grains of dust that punched through thin aluminum.

facts.label: Launched
facts.value: 16 February, 25 May and 30 July 1965, Cape Kennedy

facts.label: Wings
facts.value: 29.3 by 4.3 m, roughly 200 m² of detectors

facts.label: Orbits
facts.value: About 500 to 740 km up; Pegasus 3 nearly circular at about 530 km

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: About 1,450 kg; 10,500 kg with the rocket stage it stayed on

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (Marshall Space Flight Center; built by Fairchild)

firsts: First working payload carried by a Saturn rocket
First night launch of a Saturn (Pegasus 2)

sections.heading: Why count meteoroids
sections.text: In 1962 Apollo’s designers knew little about the grains of dust that could pierce a spacecraft’s skin. Telescopes and radar followed meteors heavier than about a ten-thousandth of a gram, and small satellites such as Explorer 16 had counted hits on thin pressurized cans. In between lay the sizes that mattered for a hull or a propellant tank, and there the estimates differed by a factor of nearly a thousand. Marshall Space Flight Center proposed a satellite big enough to catch these rarer grains, launched on a Saturn I, and Fairchild won the contract to build it in 1963.

sections.heading: The wings
sections.text: Each Pegasus rode folded inside a dummy Apollo service module on top of the Saturn I’s second stage. In orbit the boilerplate Apollo command and service modules were cast off into an orbit of their own, and a motor unfolded two wings 29.3 m long and 4.3 m wide. They held 208 detector panels: aluminum sheets 0.038, 0.2 or 0.4 mm thick over a thin plastic film and a layer of copper, each pair forming a capacitor. A grain that punched through shorted it for an instant, the spark burned the short away, and the hit was counted and timed. The satellite stayed fixed to the spent stage.

sections.heading: Three flights
sections.text: Pegasus 1 went up on 16 February 1965, the first working payload a Saturn had carried, and a television camera on board watched its wings unfold. Pegasus 2 followed at 2:35 a.m. on 25 May, the first Saturn launched at night, and Pegasus 3 on 30 July on the last Saturn I. Shorted panels troubled the first satellite, and its successors carried fixes. By the end of 1965 Pegasus 2 and 3 alone had recorded 387 penetrations of the thinnest sheets, 41 of the middle ones and 201 of the thickest. All three were switched off in August 1968.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Designers now had a measured rate instead of a guess. Near the Earth, a square meter of 0.4 mm aluminum was punctured about once in 200 days, and a square meter of the thinnest foil about once in five. The rates fell between the estimates then in use, and in December 1965 NASA announced that the structure of Apollo and its Saturn would withstand meteoroids. The hazard did not vanish: Apollo’s spacesuits kept an outer garment against heat and micrometeoroids. Pegasus 3 also carried sample panels for a Gemini spacewalker to collect, but no flight went to it, and it reentered on 4 August 1969.

pages.title: The first spacewalks: Leonov and White
pages.summary: Two men leave their spacecraft within three months, and both struggle to get back in.

facts.label: Crew
facts.value: Pavel Belyayev, Alexei Leonov; James McDivitt, Edward White

firsts: First spacewalk (Leonov)
First American spacewalk (White)
First use of a hand-held maneuvering gun in space

sections.heading: Leonov goes out
sections.text: On 18 March 1965 Voskhod 2 carried Pavel Belyayev and Alexei Leonov into orbit. Their cabin could not be emptied of air, so it had an inflatable airlock, Volga, fixed to the hatch. On the second orbit Leonov climbed through it and pushed off on a tether, the first person to float free in space. He spent about 12 minutes outside the spacecraft, turning slowly at the end of his line, while cameras filmed him with the Earth below. Belyayev followed him from inside and watched over the airlock.

sections.heading: The hard way back
sections.text: In the vacuum Leonov’s suit swelled until it was stiff, and he could no longer bend it enough to get into the airlock. Without asking the ground, he let out air to bring the pressure down, a risk of the bends. He later remembered diving in head first and turning around inside the narrow tube to close the hatch, though film of the moment seems to show him entering feet first. He was drenched in sweat. Then the automatic landing failed, the crew fired the engine by hand, and they came down in snowy forest north of Perm, where they spent two nights before rescuers reached them on skis.

sections.heading: White and the gun
sections.text: On 3 June 1965 Gemini 4 launched with James McDivitt and Edward White. Gemini had no airlock: the whole cabin was emptied and White stood up through his hatch over the Pacific. He carried a small gun that fired jets of oxygen, the first try at steering a person in space. Its gas ran out after about three minutes, and after that he moved by pulling on his gold-wrapped tether and twisting his body. McDivitt photographed him from his window, the blue Earth below and the sky black.

sections.heading: Not wanting to come in
sections.text: White enjoyed it so much that he stayed out longer than planned, about 23 minutes in all. With the spacecraft heading into darkness, the ground ordered them to end it, and McDivitt had to coax him back. White called it the saddest moment of his life. Getting the hatch shut was a struggle for both of them. These two short walks showed that people could live and work outside a spacecraft, and that doing it well would take far better suits, handholds and training, which Gemini spent the next year learning.

pages.title: Mariner 4: the first pictures of Mars
pages.summary: The first close-up pictures of another planet show Mars cratered like the Moon.

facts.label: At Mars
facts.value: Flew past on 15 July 1965 (UT; 14 July in California), 9,846 km above the surface

firsts: First spacecraft to fly past Mars
First close-up pictures of another planet

sections.heading: The flight
sections.text: Mariner 4 left Cape Canaveral on 28 November 1964 on an Atlas-Agena rocket. Its twin, Mariner 3, had been lost three weeks earlier when the shroud over its nose failed to come off, so the second craft carried the whole hope of the mission. After 228 days in space it swept past Mars on the evening of 14 July 1965, American time, at a closest distance of 9,846 km. It never stopped: everything it learned had to be gathered in that one pass, the camera starting about 42 minutes before the closest approach, and sent home afterwards.

sections.heading: Twenty-one pictures
sections.text: During the pass the television camera took 21 full pictures and part of a 22nd, a strip running from the northern lands toward the southern night, about one percent of the planet. They went onto a tape recorder, and once the craft was clear of Mars the slow work of sending them home began. The radio sent 8.33 bits each second, so a single small picture took many hours, and every one was sent twice. The playback ran until 3 August. In all the mission returned about 5.2 million bits, less than a single photograph from a modern phone.

sections.heading: What it found
sections.text: The pictures showed craters, old and battered, much like the Moon. One frame caught a crater 151 km across, now named Mariner. There were no canals and no sign of life. As the craft passed behind Mars, its radio signal shone through the edge of the atmosphere, and the way it faded showed the air to be very thin, with a surface pressure of only 4 to 7 millibars, about one percent of Earth's. Daytime temperatures were near minus 100 degrees Celsius, and the instruments found no magnetic field. Landers would need more than parachutes to slow down.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: When the first numbers came in, the engineers at JPL could not wait for the official picture. A machine printed the values as digits on paper strips; staff pinned the strips side by side and colored them by hand, like painting by numbers, then framed the result for the laboratory's director, William Pickering. It was the first look at another world from close by. The pictures ended the old dream of a Mars much like the Earth and shaped every mission that followed. Mariner 4 kept working long after, and contact ended in December 1967, after its control gas ran out.

pages.title: Pioneers 6 to 9: weather reports from the Sun
pages.summary: Four small probes circled the Sun and sent solar weather reports for Apollo.

facts.label: Launched
facts.value: 16 December 1965, 17 August 1966, 13 December 1967 and 8 November 1968, Cape Kennedy

facts.label: Orbits
facts.value: Around the Sun, between about 0.75 and 1.12 AU (the Earth is at 1 AU)

firsts: First space-based solar weather network

sections.heading: The solar wind
sections.text: In 1958 the physicist Eugene Parker argued that the Sun’s outer atmosphere streams away into space without pause. Not everyone believed him. Soviet Luna probes and NASA’s Explorer 10 picked up signs of a flow, but the proof came from Mariner 2 on its way to Venus in 1962. It found a wind that never stopped, at about 400 to 700 km/s, with fast and slow streams that came around again roughly every 27 days, as if their sources turned with the Sun. Storms in the Earth’s magnetic field rose and fell with them.

sections.heading: Four probes around the Sun
sections.text: NASA’s Ames Research Center then managed a set of small spinning probes to watch that wind from several places at once. Four were launched on Delta rockets between December 1965 and November 1968. Each went into its own orbit around the Sun, close to the Earth’s: Pioneers 6 and 9 a little inside it, Pioneers 7 and 8 a little outside, so that they drifted apart along the Earth’s path. They measured the wind’s particles, the magnetic field it carries out from the Sun, and cosmic rays; Pioneers 8 and 9 also counted dust. Each was planned to work for six months.

sections.heading: Solar weather for Apollo
sections.text: During the Apollo flights to the Moon the Pioneers sent hourly reports on the Sun’s activity, and their data went to flight controllers in Houston as a warning of bursts of solar protons that could endanger astronauts beyond the Earth’s magnetic shield. At Ames a console showed the wind’s speed, cosmic ray activity and the magnetic field at each probe. NASA’s rules for Apollo waited for particle sensors on spacecraft in solar and Earth orbit to confirm an event before acting, since only about one large flare in five sent particles toward the Earth and Moon. No major solar particle event struck during an Apollo mission.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: The Pioneers turned the solar wind from a discovery into something watched every day. Their readings were used to forecast solar storms for about a thousand users, among them the Federal Aviation Agency, airlines, power companies and communication companies. They also outlived their six months by decades. In August 1972 they and Pioneer 10, then 2.2 AU from the Sun on its way to Jupiter, followed one large solar flare together. Pioneer 9 was heard until 1983, Pioneer 7 until 1995, Pioneer 8 until 1996, and Pioneer 6 answered for the last time on 8 December 2000, 35 years after launch.

pages.title: Luna 9: the first pictures from the Moon
pages.summary: The first soft landing on the Moon, and the first look around from its surface.

facts.label: Craft
facts.value: Luna 9, with a 99 kg ball-shaped lander

firsts: First soft landing on the Moon
First pictures from the surface of another world

sections.heading: The landing
sections.text: Luna 9 left Baikonur on 31 January 1966 on a Molniya-M rocket. Eleven Soviet attempts to land gently on the Moon had already failed, and this was the twelfth. About 75 km above the Ocean of Storms its engine fired to kill most of its speed. Just above the ground a probe touched the surface and the craft threw off its lander, a ball 58 cm across wrapped in inflated bags. On 3 February 1966 the ball came to rest a few meters away on the lunar plain, shed its bags and opened its petals, which set it upright and steady.

sections.heading: The pictures
sections.text: Telemetry began a few minutes after touchdown, but the team waited about seven hours for the Sun to climb higher over the landing site. Early on 4 February the first panorama started to arrive, built up slowly by a television camera on top of the lander. Over three days Luna 9 sent nine pictures, five of them panoramas, showing pitted ground scattered with small stones right up to the horizon. The lander tilted a little between pictures, possibly as its cooling water ran low, and the shift was enough to view some of them in stereo.

sections.heading: Seen first in Britain
sections.text: At Jodrell Bank in England, the radio observatory led by Bernard Lovell was listening to Luna 9 as well. Its staff noticed that the picture signal used the standard format newspapers relied on to send photos by radio, so the Daily Express rushed a suitable receiver to the observatory. The pictures were decoded there and printed in Britain before the Soviet press had released them. In Moscow, the official whose approval was needed was asleep, and nobody wanted to wake him. Some wondered whether the designers had chosen that format on purpose.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Some scientists had feared that the Moon was covered in deep, loose dust that would swallow any craft that landed on it. Luna 9 settled the question: it sat firmly on the surface, which could carry a heavy lander, an answer that mattered for the crews to come. Its last contact came on 6 February 1966, after seven radio sessions totaling about eight hours. Four months later the American Surveyor 1 made the second soft landing, in the same Ocean of Storms. In 1970 the place where Luna 9 came down was named Planitia Descensus, the Plain of Descent.

pages.title: Surveyor 1: the first soft landing
pages.summary: America's first lander on the Moon shows that the ground will hold a spacecraft.

facts.label: Craft
facts.value: Surveyor 1, built by Hughes for JPL

facts.label: Landed
facts.value: 2 June 1966, 06:17 UT (1 June in California), Ocean of Storms

firsts: First American spacecraft to land softly on the Moon
First American pictures from the Moon's surface

sections.heading: The way down
sections.text: Surveyor 1 left Cape Kennedy on 30 May 1966 on an Atlas-Centaur and flew straight at the Moon without first entering orbit. About 63 hours later, some 75 km up, its radar fired a solid-fuel retrorocket that did most of the braking in 40 seconds and then fell away. Three small engines, throttled by the radar's readings, did the rest. They shut off a few meters above the ground, and the lander dropped onto the Ocean of Storms at 06:17 UT on 2 June. In California it was still the evening of 1 June, and the scene at JPL went out live on television. Surveyor 1 was about 14 km from its target.

sections.heading: Pictures from the surface
sections.text: Thirty-six minutes after touchdown, once engineers knew the lander had survived, its first picture came in: part of the spacecraft, one of its footpads and the dark soil it stood on. Over the next twelve days the camera built up mosaics of a level plain scattered with small craters and rocks, some more than a meter across, with low mountains on the horizon. Red, green and blue filters let the team put together color views. When night fell on 14 June the lander went quiet, but in July it answered again and sent hundreds more. In all, Surveyor 1 returned 11,240 pictures.

sections.heading: What Apollo needed to know
sections.text: Nobody yet knew for certain how firm the lunar plains were, or whether a heavy spacecraft would sink into them. Surveyor 1 answered with its own body. Strain gauges in its three legs recorded the jolt of landing, and its pictures showed the footpads pressed only slightly into the soil. Together they told engineers that the surface could bear a spacecraft's weight. The lander also measured how the ground reflected radar and how hot and cold it became. This was the kind of evidence, from Surveyor 1 and the landers that followed, that let Apollo's planners trust the ground at the sites they chose.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: The Soviet Luna 9 had reached the surface four months earlier, cushioned by air bags. Surveyor 1 was the first to land the way Apollo would, steering and braking with its engines almost to the ground, and it did so on the first try. Of the six Surveyors launched after it, four more landed safely. In 1969 the crew of Apollo 12 set down beside Surveyor 3 and brought parts of it home to see how more than two years on the Moon had changed them. Surveyor 1 still stands where it landed, inside the crater Flamsteed P, and an orbiting camera found it there in 2009.

pages.title: Lunar Orbiter 1: the Earth from the Moon
pages.summary: Scouting landing sites for Apollo, and turning around for the first view of Earth.
firsts: First US spacecraft to orbit the Moon
First picture of the Earth from the Moon’s vicinity

sections.heading: The flight
sections.text: Lunar Orbiter 1 left Cape Kennedy on an Atlas-Agena D on 10 August 1966 and went into orbit around the Moon on 14 August, the first American spacecraft to do so. The Soviet Luna 10 had got there that April. NASA’s Langley center ran the program, with Boeing building the spacecraft. The goal was practical: Apollo needed safe, smooth places to land, and someone had to look at them closely first. Controllers lowered the orbit step by step to bring the camera nearer the ground.

sections.heading: The pictures
sections.text: Over two weeks the orbiter photographed all nine candidate Apollo landing sites, more sites on the far side and the place where Surveyor 1 had touched down in June. Its pictures covered about five million square kilometers. A fault blurred many of the sharpest frames, but the medium-resolution ones were the best views of the lunar surface yet. On 23 August 1966, in a shot that was not in the plan, the spacecraft turned its camera from the Moon to catch a crescent Earth above the lunar horizon.

sections.heading: A spy camera at the Moon
sections.text: Lunar Orbiter carried no television camera in the usual sense. It exposed real film, developed it on board, then scanned each frame with a spot of light and radioed the result to Earth in strips, which were pieced together into prints on the ground. The camera, built by Eastman Kodak, came from a system made for an American reconnaissance satellite, a link kept secret until after the Cold War. The method was slow, but it gave far more detail than any television camera of the day.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Lunar Orbiter 1 was the first of five. Its successors photographed more candidate sites and, by the end of 1967, nearly the whole Moon, the maps Apollo crews trained and landed with. In November 1966 Lunar Orbiter 2 looked sideways across the crater Copernicus instead of straight down, a view of cliffs and peaks that the press called a picture of the century. The orbiter itself was crashed into the far side on 29 October 1966, so its radio would not interfere with the next one.

pages.title: Lunar Orbiter: counting meteoroid hits
pages.summary: Gas cells and dosimeters on five orbiters size up the dangers Apollo would meet.

facts.label: Detectors
facts.value: 20 pressurized cells per craft, 0.186 m² in all

facts.label: Dosimeters
facts.value: Two per craft, behind light and heavier shielding

firsts: First American measurements of meteoroids and radiation in orbit around the Moon

sections.heading: Cells around the middle
sections.text: Besides their cameras, all five Lunar Orbiters carried two small experiments from NASA’s Langley center. Charles Gurtler and William Kinnard designed the meteoroid detector: twenty half-cylinders of beryllium copper foil, 0.025 mm thick, mounted around the craft’s middle deck outside its thermal blanket. Gas inside each cell held a switch closed. A grain that punched through the foil let the gas out, the switch opened, and the next telemetry reading showed a new hole. When the builder, Boeing, planned to cut the cells to fifteen, Gurtler insisted that fewer than twenty would not give useful results.

sections.heading: Counting the hits
sections.text: Lunar Orbiter 1 reached the Moon in August 1966 and recorded no hits at all. Lunar Orbiter 2 counted three in its first nineteen days, in November, possibly grains from the Leonid meteor shower. Over 17 months the five orbiters flew equatorial and polar orbits between 30 and 6,200 km up, and together recorded 22 punctures. That came to about 0.16 per square meter per day, roughly half the rate the same kind of cells had measured on the Explorer 16 and 23 satellites near the Earth. More holes came on the side facing forward along the Earth and Moon’s path around the Sun, and the rate did not rise closer to the surface.

sections.heading: Dosimeters for the film
sections.text: Trutz Foelsche at Langley designed the radiation experiment, chiefly to protect the film. A strong burst of particles from the Sun could fog the pictures still waiting to be developed, and live readings would let controllers react in time. Each orbiter had two detectors, one behind thin aluminum, the other behind ten times as much. Crossing the Van Allen belts, the early orbiters recorded 0.75 rads at the film supply, and Lunar Orbiter 4 recorded 5.5 rads in May 1967. Between August 1966 and August 1967 the dosimeters caught several solar particle events, among them those of September 1966, January 1967 and May 1967.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Before these flights, estimates of the meteoroid hazard near the Moon ranged from somewhat less than near the Earth to many times greater. The orbiters found it no greater, the answer Apollo’s planners needed to judge how much protection its spacecraft, instruments and spacesuits required. The radiation data were translated into doses for people: the solar events had mattered only behind thin shielding, in a spacesuit or the lunar module. The analysis concluded that Apollo’s hardware would protect its crews from average and larger short-term events, but that a rare storm like those of 1959 and 1960 could be dangerous to an astronaut in a suit if no precautions were taken.

pages.title: Mascons: the Moon’s uneven pull
pages.summary: Tracking the Lunar Orbiters reveals heavy masses under the maria that bend orbits.

facts.label: Craft
facts.value: Lunar Orbiters 1 to 5, tracked by radio

facts.label: Found by
facts.value: Paul Muller and William Sjogren, JPL

firsts: Discovery of mascons, the mass concentrations under the lunar maria

sections.heading: Orbits that wandered
sections.text: Every Lunar Orbiter carried a transponder that returned radio signals from the tracking stations, so engineers could measure its speed and distance from the shifts in the signal. Small changes in an orbit showed how the Moon’s gravity pulled on the craft. The first orbiter already hinted that the Moon was slightly pear-shaped. In December 1966 controllers tilted Lunar Orbiter 2’s orbit to gather new gravity data, and the last two orbiters circled over the poles. The orbits drifted in ways that, at first, nobody could predict, and the tracking went on until Lunar Orbiter 5 was crashed into the Moon in January 1968.

sections.heading: Weights under the seas
sections.text: At the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Paul Muller and William Sjogren worked the tracking data into a gravity map of the Moon’s near side. Although their model was simple, the result was clear: there were large concentrations of mass beneath the round, ringed maria, which pulled harder on a passing spacecraft. They published it in Science on 16 August 1968 and called the features mascons. A Soviet scientist had noted from Luna 10’s orbit in 1966 that the Moon’s gravity was uneven, but NASA’s history of deep space flight credits the discovery to Muller and Sjogren. In 2013 NASA’s GRAIL mission confirmed that the mascons came from ancient giant impacts.

sections.heading: Apollo 11 lands long
sections.text: Apollo crews flew low around the Moon, and on 20 July 1969 Eagle began its descent several kilometers farther along its track than planned. Armstrong steered past a boulder field and landed long, and Houston estimated the miss at about four miles (6 km). Afterwards the flight controllers found several causes. The largest was air left in the tunnel between Eagle and Columbia, which gave Eagle a small push when the two separated; the gravity model then in use was among the others. One flight dynamics officer thought the mascons played a part. Armstrong noted that the mascons’ pull on orbits was still a concern for anyone aiming at an exact spot.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: For Apollo 12 the target was Surveyor 3, which had landed in 1967. Ground controllers measured Intrepid’s path from Earth and, a new step for Apollo 12, radioed a correction during the descent that moved its landing point 4,200 feet (about 1.3 km) downrange. Intrepid came down less than 200 meters from Surveyor. Mascons kept mattering: by the time of Apollo 15 and 17, which landed far from the equator, orbits there could still not be predicted with confidence. In 1972 the Moon’s gravity so disturbed the low orbit of a small satellite left by Apollo 16 that it struck the surface after 34 days instead of a year.

pages.title: Surveyor 3: digging into the Moon
pages.summary: A lander scoops trenches in the lunar soil, and two astronauts later walk up to it.

facts.label: Craft
facts.value: Surveyor 3, built by Hughes for JPL

facts.label: Landed
facts.value: 20 April 1967, after three touchdowns, Ocean of Storms

facts.label: Scoop work
facts.value: Four trenches, the deepest about 18 cm

firsts: First Surveyor to carry a scoop to dig into the Moon’s surface

sections.heading: Three landings and a scoop
sections.text: Surveyor 3 left Cape Kennedy on 17 April 1967. On the way down to the Ocean of Storms, bright reflections confused its radar, and its engines did not shut off at 4.3 m as planned. It touched down, bounced about 20 m, touched down again and hopped another 11 m before controllers on Earth cut the engines. It settled on 20 April on a sloping wall inside a crater about 200 m across. In place of the earlier landers’ approach camera it carried a scoop 12 cm long on a 1.5 m folding arm, which engineers on Earth drove by radio command, in short timed steps, while the lander’s camera watched.

sections.heading: Testing the ground
sections.text: In 1955 the astronomer Thomas Gold had proposed that the Moon’s smooth plains were dust that had settled flat, and some feared such dust would not hold a spacecraft. Luna 9 and Surveyor 1 had already stood on the surface. Surveyor 3 tested it. Over 18 hours of work the scoop dug four trenches, the deepest about 18 cm, pressed into the soil, dropped onto it and squeezed a small rock without breaking it. The soil behaved much like moist, fine-grained soil on Earth. It was softer at the surface and firmer about 10 cm down, and the footpads had sunk no more than 5 cm. The camera sent back more than 6,300 pictures before the lunar night fell.

sections.heading: Visitors from Apollo 12
sections.text: Surveyor 3 never woke after its first lunar night, but its site was chosen for Apollo 12, a chance to show that a crew could land on a chosen spot. On 19 November 1969 Pete Conrad and Alan Bean set Intrepid down on the crater’s rim, 155 m away. The next day they walked down the slope and spent about 25 minutes at the lander. Its trenches and footpad prints looked much as they had in 1967. With cutters they removed the camera, the scoop with some soil still inside, and lengths of tubing and cable. Studies on Earth later showed that dust blown by Intrepid’s engine had sandblasted the old lander.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: The lunar module’s legs had been designed before anyone knew what the surface was like. Its engineers assumed soil that a static load of about 7 kPa would press in no more than 10 cm. The soil Surveyor 3 tested bore 20 to 55 kPa, and the Surveyor and Lunar Orbiter results confirmed that the assumed surface was a sound basis. Apollo 11 then showed it to be on the cautious side: its footpads sank only 1 to 4 cm. The parts that Apollo 12 brought home showed that the camera’s electronics, optics and mechanisms had come through 31 months on the Moon in good condition. The camera is now at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum.

pages.title: Venera 4 and Mariner 5: into the air of Venus
pages.summary: A Soviet capsule falls silent in Venus’s air; a US flyby shows how deep that air goes.

facts.label: Craft
facts.value: Venera 4, a carrier with a descent capsule; Mariner 5, a flyby craft

facts.label: Descent
facts.value: 93 minutes of readings from Venera 4’s capsule

firsts: First craft to send back data from inside another planet’s atmosphere (Venera 4)

sections.heading: Venera 4 goes in
sections.text: Venera 4 left Baikonur on a Molniya rocket on 12 June 1967. Built by the Lavochkin design bureau, it carried a descent capsule, a sphere about 1 m across with a mass of 383 kg, made to stand up to the heat and the braking of entry. On 18 October it reached Venus and let the capsule go, and the carrier burned up in the atmosphere behind it. The capsule hit the night side at about 11 km/s, slowed behind a thick heat shield, and opened its main parachute about 52 km up. For 93 minutes it radioed back temperature, pressure, density and the makeup of the air around it.

sections.heading: The silence
sections.text: What it found was startling. The air was 90 to 95 percent carbon dioxide, with none of the nitrogen many had expected to make up most of it, and it grew steadily hotter on the way down, past 260 °C. The barometer, built to read no more than 7.3 atmospheres, soon ran off its scale. Then the signal stopped. Soviet scientists at first announced that the capsule had kept transmitting until it touched the ground, so its last readings would be the surface itself. Later analysis showed it had gone silent some 25 km or more above the ground, overwhelmed by heat and pressure or out of battery power.

sections.heading: Mariner 5 the next day
sections.text: Mariner 5, the spare Mariner 4, was rebuilt for Venus and launched from Cape Kennedy on 14 June 1967. It carried no camera. On 19 October, a day after Venera 4, it passed about 4,000 km above Venus and slipped behind the planet as seen from Earth for some 26 minutes. Going in and coming out, its radio signal passed through the atmosphere, which bent and weakened it. From those changes JPL’s team worked out how temperature, pressure and density climbed with depth, down to where the signal was lost. Carried on down to the surface found by Earth-based radar, the profile gave a pressure 75 to 100 times Earth’s and a temperature over 500 °C.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Put side by side, the two flights told one story: matched to the radar’s surface, Venera 4’s last readings came from about 25 km up, not from the ground. American and Soviet scientists compared the data in Arizona in March 1968, at one of the first international meetings on results from planetary spacecraft. Lavochkin built stronger capsules. Venera 5 and 6, made for 25 atmospheres, still went silent about 18 km up, so Venera 7 was built for 150 to 180 atmospheres and 540 °C. On 15 December 1970 it sent back the first signals from the surface of another planet: about 90 atmospheres and 475 °C, a good fit with the 1967 estimates.

pages.title: Zond 5: tortoises around the Moon
pages.summary: Two tortoises flew around the Moon and back, the first living things to do so.

facts.label: Craft
facts.value: Zond 5 (7K-L1 no. 9), a circumlunar ship without its crew

facts.label: Launch vehicle
facts.value: Proton-K with a Blok D upper stage

facts.label: At the Moon
facts.value: 18 September 1968, about 1,950 km from the far side

facts.label: Crew
facts.value: None; two steppe tortoises, fly eggs, mealworms, seeds, plants and bacteria

firsts: First spacecraft to fly around the Moon and return to Earth
First living things to travel around the Moon

sections.heading: The passengers
sections.text: The 7K-L1 was the Soviet ship for sending two cosmonauts around the Moon, and Zond 5 flew one with animals and plants in their place. The main passengers were two steppe tortoises, each weighing 340 to 400 grams, chosen because they could be held firmly in place and needed little life support. They went aboard on 2 September and were given no food from then on, as were control tortoises on the ground, so that doctors could tell the effects of fasting from those of the flight. Fruit fly eggs, mealworms, seeds, a flowering plant, algae and bacteria flew too, and a dummy fitted with radiation detectors sat in the pilot’s seat.

sections.heading: Around the Moon
sections.text: A Proton rocket put the ship into Earth orbit, and about 67 minutes after launch its upper stage fired again to send it toward the Moon. On the way, the star sensor needed for steering failed, fouled by residue from the ship’s own coatings. Controllers made a course correction on 17 September with less precise Sun and Earth sensors, 325,000 km from home. On 18 September Zond 5 swung around the far side, about 1,950 km above the surface. Its cameras also photographed the whole Earth from about 90,000 km out. At Jodrell Bank, British listeners even heard a voice reading out instrument values: cosmonauts on the ground, rehearsing through the ship.

sections.heading: Straight down
sections.text: On the way back an Earth sensor failed too, and the ship’s stabilizer switched off its guided reentry, the path planned to bring it down on Soviet land. Instead controllers spent about twenty hours nudging the ship with small thrusters until it lined up with a narrow corridor for a steep, ballistic entry over the Indian Ocean, the backup area. The capsule opened its parachutes at 7 km and splashed down at night on 21 September 1968, 105 km from the nearest Soviet ship. U.S. Navy vessels watched as a Soviet ship found it hours later. It reached Bombay by sea on 3 October and Moscow by air.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: The tortoises came back alive, the first living things to have flown around the Moon. They had lost about a tenth of their weight but stayed active and hungry, and dissection showed that most of the changes in their bodies came from fasting, not from the flight. Zond 5 proved that a ship could return from the Moon and that living things could survive the trip, even its rough, steep reentry. The Soviets began planning a crewed flight around the Moon. In the United States, NASA had been studying since August whether to send Apollo 8 to the Moon; Zond 5 added to the pressure, and on 12 November NASA announced that it would.

pages.title: Apollo 8: Earthrise
pages.summary: The first people to leave Earth orbit circle the Moon ten times at Christmas.

facts.label: At the Moon
facts.value: 24 to 25 December 1968, ten orbits in about 20 hours

facts.label: Crew

First crewed flight of the Saturn V
First people to see the Earth rise over the Moon

sections.heading: The flight
sections.text: Apollo 8 was meant to test the lunar module close to Earth. When the lander ran late in the summer of 1968, NASA chose a bolder plan: send the command ship alone to the Moon. Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and Bill Anders left Florida on 21 December 1968, riding the first Saturn V ever to carry a crew. Three days later they fired their engine behind the Moon, out of radio contact, and slipped into orbit. For about twenty hours they circled ten times, mapping and photographing the surface from about 110 km up, before firing the engine again for home.

sections.heading: Earthrise
sections.text: On their fourth time around, the crew rolled the spacecraft and saw the Earth coming up over the gray lunar horizon. Nobody had planned for it. Anders took a black-and-white frame, then asked for a magazine of color film and took two more through a side window. The flight journal's reconstruction credits all three to Anders, though Borman later remembered taking one himself. The second of them, a small blue and white Earth over a barren foreground, became one of the most reproduced photographs ever taken, and many people credit it with helping to change how we see our own planet.

sections.heading: Christmas Eve
sections.text: That evening, on the ninth orbit, the crew went on live television. They showed the lunar surface sliding past below and described what they saw. Then, as the spacecraft crossed into lunar night, Borman had planned a closing: each man read in turn from the opening verses of the Book of Genesis, Anders first, then Lovell, then Borman. Borman ended with good night, good luck and a Merry Christmas to everyone on the good Earth. Before the broadcast he had told the others that more people might be listening than had ever listened to anyone.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Apollo 8 proved that the Saturn V could carry people, that the navigation could find the Moon and that a crew could fire into lunar orbit and back out again with nobody to help them on the far side. Every later Apollo flight built on what it learned. It came at the end of a hard year, and the pictures of a small, whole Earth gave many people something to share. The crew splashed down in the Pacific on 27 December, and seven months later Apollo 11 followed their path to land.

pages.title: Apollo 11: Tranquility Base
pages.summary: Armstrong and Aldrin land on the Moon and walk on it while Collins waits in orbit.

facts.label: Crew
facts.value: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, Michael Collins

firsts: First people to land on the Moon
First steps on another world
First samples of the Moon brought to Earth

sections.heading: The descent
sections.text: Apollo 11 left Florida on 16 July 1969 and reached lunar orbit three days later. On 20 July Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin undocked in the lunar module Eagle and started down, leaving Michael Collins alone in Columbia. The way down was not smooth. The guidance computer flashed alarms, 1202 and then 1201, because it was being asked to do more than it had time for, and Mission Control judged it safe to carry on. Near the bottom Armstrong saw that the computer was taking them into a crater ringed with boulders, took over by hand and flew on, looking for a clear patch.

sections.heading: The Eagle has landed
sections.text: Fuel was running low. A warning light came on, and Houston began counting down the seconds left before the crew would have to land or abort. Then Aldrin called "Contact light": a probe under a footpad had touched the surface. It was 20:17 UT on 20 July 1969, a summer afternoon in America, and Eagle had less than a minute of usable fuel to spare. Armstrong reported: "Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed." Charlie Duke, the capsule communicator, tripped over the new name before answering that they had a bunch of guys about to turn blue, and were breathing again.

sections.heading: On the surface
sections.text: Armstrong stepped down from the ladder at 02:56 UT on 21 July, still the evening of 20 July in America, and said, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." He later said he had meant "for a man". Aldrin followed him. In a little over two hours outside they planted a flag, took photographs, collected 21.55 kg of rock and soil, and set out a seismometer, a laser reflector and a sheet of foil to catch particles from the Sun. The flag gave them trouble: the ground was hard a few inches down. "Six to eight inches was about as far as I could get it in," Armstrong said after the flight. Together they spent about 21 and a half hours on the Moon before Eagle's upper stage lifted off to rejoin Columbia.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: In May 1961 President Kennedy had asked for a landing on the Moon, and a safe return, before the decade was out. Apollo 11 met that goal with five months to spare, and its crew splashed down in the Pacific on 24 July 1969. The flight was followed live on radio and television around the world. The rocks it brought home began the science of lunar samples, and the questions they raised, about how the Moon formed and how old its surface is, sent the later Apollo crews to very different places.

pages.title: Mariners 6 and 7: the thin air of Mars
pages.summary: Twin flybys measure the thin carbon dioxide air of Mars and find its polar cap frozen.

sections.heading: Two craft, one plan
sections.text: Mariners 6 and 7 were twins, built at JPL to study Mars from close by and to prepare the way for later missions. Ten days before launch, the Atlas meant for Mariner 6 began to buckle on the pad when a faulty switch let its tanks lose pressure, until two ground crewmen stopped the leak; the probe moved to another rocket and left Cape Kennedy on 25 February 1969. Mariner 7 followed on 27 March. Mariner 6 swept past Mars on 31 July at about 3,430 km, over the equatorial regions. Its views of the south polar cap led controllers to reprogram Mariner 7 for more of them before it passed on 5 August.

sections.heading: Listening through the air
sections.text: Neither craft carried anything to drop into the atmosphere. The measurement came from the radio. As each Mariner passed behind Mars, its signal grazed the edge of the planet on the way in and again on the way out, four soundings in all. How much the gas bent the signal showed how dense it was, all the way down to the ground. For air mostly of carbon dioxide, three points gave a surface pressure of 6 to 7 millibars, less than one percent of Earth’s at sea level. The fourth gave only 3.8, which the team read as ground 5 to 6 km higher. Mariner 4 had found 4 to 7 millibars in 1965; two more craft now confirmed it.

sections.heading: Carbon dioxide, even frozen
sections.text: The other instruments read the light from Mars. An ultraviolet spectrometer saw the glow of ionized carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide high in the atmosphere, and the light of atomic hydrogen and oxygen. An infrared radiometer found the south polar cap as cold as 150 kelvin, about minus 123 degrees Celsius, a sign that the cap was frozen carbon dioxide. Mariner 7’s infrared spectrometer caught sharp bands at the cap’s edge that matched methane and ammonia, but the team traced them to carbon dioxide ice. The cameras showed cratered ground across the south, a jumbled “chaotic” terrain, and the floor of Hellas, where the cameras could make out no craters.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Three flybys now agreed: the pressure at the surface of Mars was about a hundredth of Earth’s, and lower still on high ground. Viking was designed around it. The 1969 results shaped Viking’s entry shell, 3.5 meters across: braking in the air was the only practical way to slow so heavy a lander. Each Viking came in behind an ablative heat shield, opened a 16-meter parachute about 6 km up and fired retro-rockets for the last 1.5 km. Its parachute was tested by balloon drops over New Mexico in 1972, and its planners looked for low ground, where the air is thickest.

pages.title: Luna 16: Moon soil by robot
pages.summary: A robot lands, drills into the Moon and sends 101 grams of soil back to Earth.

facts.label: Craft
facts.value: Luna 16, a lander with a return rocket

facts.label: Sample
facts.value: 101 g, drilled from about 35 cm deep

firsts: First robotic return of a sample from the Moon
First landing on the Moon during the lunar night

sections.heading: The flight
sections.text: Luna 16 left Baikonur on 12 September 1970 on a Proton rocket. Soviet engineers had been trying to bring back Moon soil by robot, and five attempts in a row had failed. The best known was Luna 15, which crashed into the Sea of Crises on 21 July 1969, about two hours before Apollo 11’s crew lifted off from the Moon with their own samples. Luna 16 went into orbit around the Moon on 17 September and landed in the Sea of Fertility on 20 September 1970, some 60 hours after sunset there.

sections.heading: Drilling in the dark
sections.text: Less than an hour after touchdown, an arm lowered a drill to the ground. It bored for seven minutes and stopped about 35 cm down, then swung its core up in an arc and dropped it into a small round capsule at the top of the spacecraft, where it was sealed in. A little of the soil seems to have spilled on the way. The cameras had tried to show the site, but in the dark the pictures were of little use. On 21 September the upper stage fired its engine and lifted off, leaving the lander behind.

sections.heading: Coming home
sections.text: The return rocket made no course corrections at all. Its path back had been worked out in advance, and three days later, on 24 September 1970, the capsule hit the atmosphere at nearly 11 km per second, braking at up to 350 times the force of gravity. It weighed about 34 kg and came down under a parachute about 80 km southeast of Dzhezkazgan in Kazakhstan. Inside were 101 grams of dark lunar soil: fine, well-worn rock from the lava plains, full of glass, with fragments billions of years old.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Luna 16 did with machines what Apollo had done with astronauts: it landed, gathered soil and brought it home. No one had to leave Earth to do it. Its soil looked much like Apollo 12’s, and samples went to scientists abroad. On 10 June 1971 Soviet and American scientists met in Moscow and exchanged samples, Luna 16 soil for some from Apollo 11 and 12. Luna 20 and Luna 24 followed in 1972 and 1976, and NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter later found the landing stages of all three.

pages.title: Lunokhod 1: a rover on the Moon
pages.summary: The first rover on another world, driven across the Moon from Earth for ten months.

facts.label: Craft
facts.value: Luna 17 lander with the Lunokhod 1 rover

firsts: First rover to drive on another world

sections.heading: The landing
sections.text: Luna 17 left Baikonur on a Proton rocket on 10 November 1970 and landed on Mare Imbrium, the Sea of Rains, on 17 November. It was the second try: the first rover had been destroyed in February 1969, when its rocket broke apart less than a minute after launch. Luna 17’s landing stage carried ramps on both sides, so the rover had two ways off. Nearly three hours after touchdown, on a command from Earth, Lunokhod 1 rolled down a ramp and onto the Moon.

sections.heading: The rover
sections.text: Lunokhod 1 looked like a large tub on eight wheels, each with its own motor. It weighed 756 kg and stood about 1.35 m tall. The inside of its hinged lid was covered with solar cells that charged the batteries in daylight. Through the long lunar nights, each about two weeks, a heater warmed by radioactive polonium-210 kept the instruments from freezing. It carried television cameras for driving, cameras for panoramas, an X-ray instrument that analyzed the soil, a probe that pressed into the ground to test how firm it was, and a laser reflector supplied by France.

sections.heading: Driving from Earth
sections.text: With nobody on board, the rover was driven from a control room on Earth. Two crews of five took turns at the controls: a commander, a driver, a flight engineer, a navigator and an operator who kept the narrow-beam antenna pointed at Earth. Every command took at least four seconds to show its result, counting the signal’s round trip and the time to work the levers, so the drivers steered by pictures that were always a little out of date. The top speed was about 100 m an hour. They were nicknamed the sedentary cosmonauts.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Lunokhod 1 was designed to last three lunar days and kept going for eleven, until the last contact on 14 September 1971. In that time it drove about 10 km, sent back more than 20,000 television pictures and 206 panoramas, and tested the soil at hundreds of places. It showed that a robot could be driven on another world for months, the path later rovers on Mars would follow. In 2010 NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed it where it had stopped, and an American team bounced laser light off its French reflector once more.

pages.title: Orbiting Frog Otolith: the inner ear in orbit
pages.summary: Two bullfrogs wired at the inner ear showed how its gravity sensors adapt to orbit.

facts.label: Orbit
facts.value: 300 to 574 km, one turn in about 93 minutes

facts.label: Data
facts.value: About 144 hours of recordings from the frogs’ nerves

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (Office of Advanced Research and Technology; Ames, Wallops)

firsts: First direct recordings from the inner ear’s gravity sensors during a long stay in weightlessness

sections.heading: The question
sections.text: Deep in the inner ear, tiny crystals called otoliths rest on a bed of sensory hair cells. When the head tilts or speeds up, the crystals shift, bend the hairs and change the rate at which the nerve fires. On Earth gravity always pulls on them; in orbit it doesn’t. People in weightlessness, in aircraft and in spacecraft, had suffered from disorientation, which was blamed on this balance system, and NASA wanted to know what happened to the sensors over days rather than seconds. Bullfrogs were chosen because their otoliths work much like ours, they are small enough to pack, and they can live in water during a flight.

sections.heading: Two wired frogs
sections.text: The experiment was designed by Torquato Gualtierotti of the University of Milan while he worked at NASA’s Ames Research Center. Before launch, fine electrodes were implanted in the balance nerve of each of two bullfrogs, two per frog, each listening to a single nerve fiber. The frogs rode in a sealed package about 46 cm across, in a water-filled centrifuge that could spin them up to 50 turns a minute, about half a g, to give their ears a test pull. Heartbeat and water temperature were sent down too. After launch the spacecraft stopped its spin and unfolded four booms, which kept the frogs within a thousandth of a g of weightlessness between runs.

sections.heading: What the nerves said
sections.text: The recordings held through launch, and the frogs’ heartbeats showed them in good health throughout. In weightlessness the resting firing rate of the sensors first fell and then rose, swinging over about a day, and their response to the centrifuge became exaggerated, overshooting as it spun up and undershooting as it slowed. Over more than 100 hours the sensors adjusted, and in the last 10 to 20 hours of the flight they were back to normal. One frog’s heart signal became noisy after a day, so its data were analyzed only for the first 40 hours. The frogs were never meant to come back: recovery was not planned, and the spacecraft fell back into the atmosphere in May 1971.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: OFO-A showed that the inner ear does not simply go quiet in orbit: its gravity sensors are thrown off for the first days and then, over four to five days, adapt to the new conditions. The investigators suggested that the early changes could explain the space sickness felt by some astronauts, and warned that the same sensors would need time to readjust after a long flight back on Earth. They asked that planners allow for that when sending crews on long stays to the space stations then being prepared. NASA’s first, Skylab, was launched in 1973.

facts.value: David Scott, James Irwin, Alfred Worden

sections.heading: Over the Apennines
sections.text: Apollo 15 left Florida on 26 July 1971 with David Scott, James Irwin and Alfred Worden. It was the first of a new kind of Apollo flight, built for longer stays and wider travel. On 30 July Scott and Irwin brought the lunar module Falcon down a steeper path than any crew before, to clear the Apennine Mountains, and landed on a plain between the peaks and a winding canyon called Hadley Rille, nearly a kilometer wide. Worden stayed in orbit in Endeavour, mapping and photographing the Moon with cameras and instruments in a bay of the service module. Below him, his crewmates would stay almost three days.

sections.heading: A car for the Moon
sections.text: Folded against the side of Falcon was the Lunar Roving Vehicle, an electric car with four wheels of woven steel wire, each turned by its own motor. A dish antenna on its front sent color television straight home, from a camera that controllers in Houston could aim. On 31 July Scott took it for its first drive. Over three moonwalks the two men drove 27.8 km, along the rim of Hadley Rille and up the slopes of the mountain called Hadley Delta, going as far as 5 km from the lander. Earlier crews had gone on foot. With the rover, Apollo's geologists could send them where they most wanted to look.

sections.heading: The Genesis Rock
sections.text: On 1 August, on the slope of Hadley Delta near a small crater called Spur, Scott and Irwin spotted a pale fragment resting on a darker clod, as if set out for them. It was almost pure plagioclase, the light mineral thought to make up the Moon's first crust, and Scott sealed it in a bag of its own. By the flight home it was being called the Genesis Rock. In the laboratory, sample 15415, a 269-gram piece of anorthosite, proved to be about 4 billion years old. That is younger than the Moon itself, but it is still one of the purest pieces of the ancient highland crust ever brought to Earth.

sections.heading: A hammer and a feather
sections.text: At the end of the last moonwalk on 2 August, with the rover's camera watching, Scott held a geologist's hammer in his right hand and a falcon feather in his left, a nod to his lander's name. He recalled Galileo, who had argued that without air all things fall at the same rate, and let both go. They landed in the dust together. Hours later Falcon lifted off, and for the first time people on Earth watched a launch from the Moon live, through the rover's camera. On the way home, about 320,000 km from Earth, Worden climbed outside to fetch film from the cameras. They splashed down on 7 August.

pages.title: Mariner 9: the first orbiter of another planet
pages.summary: The first craft to orbit another planet waits out a dust storm, then maps Mars.
firsts: First spacecraft to orbit another planet
First detailed views of Phobos and Deimos

sections.heading: First into orbit
sections.text: Two Mariners were built for Mars in 1971. Mariner 8 was lost when its rocket failed on 9 May, so Mariner 9 left Cape Canaveral alone on 30 May with the work of both. After a flight of 167 days it fired its engine for a little over 15 minutes on 14 November 1971 and became the first spacecraft to orbit another planet. It beat the Soviet Mars 2, which had left Earth eleven days earlier. Its orbit swung it as close as about 1,400 km above the surface and around the planet roughly twice a day.

sections.heading: Waiting out the storm
sections.text: Mars was not ready to be seen. In September 1971 a dust storm had started in the southern highlands and grown until it wrapped the whole planet. As Mariner 9 approached, its camera found a featureless orange disk with a few dark spots. Unlike a flyby, an orbiter could wait, so the team held back the mapping and watched the dust from orbit. Through December the dust slowly settled, the dark spots turned out to be mountaintops, and in the first weeks of 1972 the real mapping began.

sections.heading: Volcanoes and a canyon
sections.text: The dark spots were the summits of giant volcanoes standing above the dust: the three of Tharsis in a row, and the largest of all, Olympus Mons, about 600 km across at its base. In all, the team identified about 20 volcanoes. As the air cleared, a system of canyons appeared that runs more than 4,000 km along the equator, nearly as long as the United States is wide. It was named Valles Marineris after the spacecraft. The pictures showed a planet far more varied than Mariner 4 had suggested, with volcanoes, canyons and old craters side by side.

sections.heading: Phobos and Deimos
sections.text: Mariner 9 also took at least 80 pictures of the two small moons of Mars, the first detailed views of either. Phobos, photographed from 5,760 km, turned out to be a lumpy, cratered rock about 26 km across at its longest, more like an asteroid than a moon. Deimos is smaller still. The spacecraft kept working until its control gas ran out, and it was switched off on 27 October 1972 after sending back 7,329 pictures, enough to map about 85 percent of Mars. It was left in an orbit expected to last at least fifty years.

pages.title: Pioneer 10: the first to Jupiter
pages.summary: First through the asteroid belt, first past Jupiter, and a plaque for whoever finds it.
firsts: First spacecraft through the asteroid belt
First to fly past Jupiter
First on a path out of the solar system

sections.heading: Through the asteroid belt
sections.text: Pioneer 10 was launched from Cape Canaveral on a three-stage Atlas-Centaur on the evening of 2 March 1972, Florida time. Leaving Earth at about 51,700 km/h, it was the fastest object people had made at the time and passed the Moon's orbit in about 11 hours. Its first test was the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Nobody knew how much grit was out there, and some feared a craft could be worn away or wrecked. Pioneer 10 entered the belt on 15 July 1972 and came out in February 1973 unharmed, having met far fewer particles than expected. The way to the outer planets was open.

sections.heading: Jupiter's radiation
sections.text: Pioneer 10 flew past Jupiter on 4 December 1973, about 130,000 km above the cloud tops. Its instruments found the planet wrapped in belts of trapped radiation, roughly ten times stronger than its planners had predicted. From 3 December, charged particles set off false commands on board, and some planned pictures were lost, among them close views of the moon Io. Ground controllers sent corrections that saved most of the sequence, and the craft came through. It also showed how far Jupiter's magnetic field reaches: its tail stretches some 800 million km behind the planet, about as far as the orbit of Saturn.

sections.heading: The pictures
sections.text: Pioneer 10 carried no camera. Its pictures came from an imaging photopolarimeter, a small telescope 2.5 cm across with one detector for red light and one for blue. The spacecraft spun as it flew, and each turn swept the telescope across the planet in a thin strip; a motor then tipped it a little for the next strip. Computers on the ground put the strips together into images, with green worked out from the red and blue. Between 6 November and 31 December 1973 it took about 500 pictures of Jupiter, the sharpest showing details about 320 km across.

sections.heading: The plaque
sections.text: Fixed to the antenna struts, where passing dust would wear it least, is a gold-anodized aluminum plate about 15 by 23 cm. Carl Sagan and Frank Drake designed it and Linda Salzman Sagan drew it. It shows a man and a woman in front of an outline of the spacecraft, the Sun and its planets with Pioneer's path leading out past Jupiter, and the Sun's place marked against 14 pulsars, with a hydrogen atom as the key to the units. The last faint signal from Pioneer 10 reached Earth on 23 January 2003, from about 12 billion km away. The plaque travels on in silence.

pages.title: Mariner 10: Mercury up close
pages.summary: Venus bends its path, then three passes show Mercury's cratered face.
firsts: First spacecraft to visit two planets
First to use one planet's gravity to reach another
First spacecraft to study Mercury

sections.heading: By way of Venus
sections.text: Mariner 10 left Cape Canaveral on an Atlas-Centaur on 3 November 1973, bound for Mercury by way of Venus. No spacecraft had yet used one planet's gravity to reach another. Instead of a bigger rocket and more fuel, the plan used Venus: the craft passed 5,768 km from the planet on 5 February 1974, and the encounter bent its course inward toward the Sun. On the way past it took more than 4,000 pictures. Through an ultraviolet filter, the bland clouds of Venus showed bands and spirals, and the cloud tops turned out to race around the planet in about four and a half days.

sections.heading: Three passes
sections.text: Giuseppe Colombo, a scientist at the University of Padua in Italy, noticed that after the first flyby Mariner 10 would circle the Sun every 176 days, twice the length of Mercury's year. With small course corrections, the craft could meet the planet again and again. It passed about 700 km from Mercury on 29 March 1974, some 48,000 km away on 21 September, and just 327 km from the surface on 16 March 1975. No spacecraft had come back to its target before. Then its attitude-control gas ran out, and contact ended on 24 March 1975.

sections.heading: A face like the Moon's
sections.text: Mariner 10 sent back the first close views of Mercury, and at first glance they looked like the Moon: craters of every age crowded together, with smooth plains between them. Long cliffs, some hundreds of kilometers long, cut across craters and plains alike. Scientists now think they rose as the planet's interior cooled and shrank. One quirk limited the map. Mercury turns three times for every two trips around the Sun, so on each pass the same side was lit. Only about 40 to 45 percent of the planet was photographed, some of it in detail as fine as about 100 meters.

sections.heading: A basin and a magnetic field
sections.text: On the first pass, half of a vast ringed basin lay along the line between day and night, more than 1,300 km across. It was named Caloris, from the word for heat, because it lies where Mercury faces the Sun at its closest. The bigger surprise came from the magnetometer. Few expected small, slowly turning Mercury to have a magnetic field, but Mariner 10 found a weak one, around a hundredth as strong as Earth's at the surface. The third and lowest pass, in March 1975, confirmed that the field was the planet's own. No spacecraft saw Mercury again until MESSENGER flew past in 2008.

pages.title: Venus's surface: Venera 9 and Venera 13
pages.summary: The first pictures from another planet's surface, then the first in color from Venus.

facts.label: Craft
facts.value: Venera 9 and Venera 13, each a carrier with a lander

firsts: First pictures from the surface of another planet (Venera 9)
First color pictures from the surface of Venus (Venera 13)

sections.heading: Venera 9
sections.text: Venera 9 was launched on a Proton rocket from Baikonur on 8 June 1975. Two days out, its lander separated from the craft that would orbit Venus and relay its signal. A heat shield, three parachutes, a drag disk and a crushable landing ring brought it down near the highland of Beta Regio on 22 October 1975. A camera cover stuck, so it saw only half the planned circle, but it sent back the first pictures ever taken on the surface of another planet: flat, sharp-edged rocks 30 to 40 cm across, clear shadows and no dust in the air. It kept working for 53 minutes, until the orbiter passed out of range.

sections.heading: The conditions
sections.text: Venus's surface is a brutal place for a machine. Venera 9 measured about 485 °C, hot enough to melt lead, and a pressure about 90 times that at sea level on Earth. Above it, a deep layer of cloud still let through about as much light as a cloudy summer day at Earth's middle latitudes. To last even an hour, the lander was cooled to −10 °C before entry by a circulating fluid that also spread the heat around, and its instruments sat inside a sealed body that the heat slowly worked its way into. Venera 13, landing further south, measured 457 °C and 89 atmospheres.

sections.heading: Venera 13 in color
sections.text: Venera 13 left Baikonur on 30 October 1981 and landed on 1 March 1982, east of the highland called Phoebe Regio. Built to last 32 minutes, it worked for 127. Its cameras could look through red, green and blue filters, so its panoramas could be put together in color: flat slabs of rock and dark soil under an orange light, with a cast-off lens cover lying on the ground. A drill took a soil sample into a sealed chamber, where an X-ray instrument found it close to a basalt rich in potassium. A sound detector picked up the noises of the lander at work and of a light wind.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Venus hides under clouds no telescope can see through, so until 1975 its surface was known only from radar and from instruments that had measured its heat and pressure. Venera 9 turned it into a place with rocks, shadows and a horizon. Venera 13 and its twin, Venera 14, which landed four days later, added color and the chemistry of the rocks. Their pictures are still the only color views from the surface of Venus, and Venera 13's 127 minutes is still the longest any lander has lasted there. Soviet engineers had built machines that could survive there, if only for an hour or two.

pages.title: Viking 1: on the surface of Mars
pages.summary: The first lander to work on Mars, and the first pictures from its surface.
firsts: First spacecraft to land on Mars and keep working
First photographs from the surface of Mars

sections.heading: The landing
sections.text: Viking 1 left Cape Canaveral on 20 August 1975 on a Titan IIIE-Centaur and reached Mars on 19 June 1976. The orbiter's pictures showed the planned landing site was rougher than expected, so the team picked a safer spot. On 20 July 1976, seven years to the day after Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, the lander separated from the orbiter and came down on the western slopes of Chryse Planitia, a wide plain north of the Martian equator. The Soviet Mars 3 had touched down in 1971 but fell silent within seconds. Viking 1 was the first to land on Mars and keep working.

sections.heading: The first pictures
sections.text: Minutes after touchdown the lander's camera started on its first picture. It did not take a snapshot but scanned the scene strip by strip. The first frame showed the ground close beside the lander: rocks, sand and dust next to footpad 2, with a little fine material thrown onto the pad by the landing. A panorama of the site followed, taken in the late Martian afternoon, showing a rock-strewn plain out to a horizon about 3 km away. The next day, 21 July, the camera scanned a view three times through color filters to make the first color picture from the surface.

sections.heading: The search for life
sections.text: From 28 July 1976 the lander's arm scooped soil into a small biology laboratory on board. Three experiments looked for living things in different ways: one fed the soil water and nutrients and watched the gases above it, one fed it nutrients marked with radioactive carbon and watched for that carbon to come back out as gas, and one checked whether soil kept under light took up carbon from a marked atmosphere. Some readings looked like life at first. But another instrument found no organic compounds in the soil, and most scientists came to explain the results by reactive chemistry in the soil. A few, among them the leader of the labeled release experiment, Gilbert Levin, never agreed.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Viking 1's lander kept working until November 1982, more than six years on the surface, sending back weather readings and pictures of the same patch of ground through the Martian seasons. With its twin, Viking 2, it returned over 1,400 images of the two landing sites, while the orbiters mapped the whole planet. The answer on life stayed open. In 2008 the Phoenix lander found perchlorate salts in Martian soil, which can destroy organic compounds when heated, as Viking's instrument heated its samples. Later the lander was named the Thomas Mutch Memorial Station, after the leader of its imaging team.
