pages.title: Vikings 1 and 2: the soil of Mars
pages.summary: Two lander arms dig into Mars and find an iron-rich, oxidizing soil with no organics.

facts.label: Landed
facts.value: 20 July 1976, Chryse Planitia; 3 September 1976, Utopia Planitia

firsts: First chemical analysis of Martian soil

sections.heading: Digging and standing
sections.text: Each lander reached out with a sampler arm: a scoop with a lid and a small backhoe on a boom about 3 m long. Its first trench at the Viking 1 site, dug on 28 July 1976, was about 8 cm wide, 5 cm deep and 15 cm long. The walls stood steep, like a trench in damp sand, although the soil was bone dry. The arm also measured how hard the ground resisted being pushed and how much dust clung to the scoop. One of Viking 1’s feet had landed in soft drift and sunk about 13 cm, with loose soil sliding over it, while another stood on firmer ground. Mechanically, the soil there was much like the Moon’s.

sections.heading: What the soil is made of
sections.text: Inside each lander, an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer lit the soil with X-rays and measured what came back, which differs for each element. The first sample from Chryse already showed the pattern: about 14 percent iron, a few percent sulfur, little aluminum. In all, the landers collected 21 samples for it, and 17 were analyzed precisely. Compared with soils on Earth and the dark plains of the Moon, Martian soil was richer in iron and far richer in sulfur and chlorine. Crusty clods held about half again as much sulfur as loose soil. And soil from the two sites, some 4,500 km apart, was nearly the same, as if dust storms had mixed it across the planet.

sections.heading: Chemistry, not life
sections.text: The biology experiments, built to look for life, ended up revealing the soil’s chemistry. When Viking 1’s gas exchange experiment only moistened a sample, it gave off about 15 times more oxygen than any known source could explain. In the labeled release experiment, nutrient marked with radioactive carbon quickly turned to radioactive gas, and heating the soil beforehand stopped the reaction. The organic analyzer found no organic compounds at either site, down to parts per billion, although heating a sample to 500 degrees Celsius drove out a lot of water. Most of the scientists came to see strong oxidizers in the soil, perhaps peroxides made by the Sun’s ultraviolet light, able to break organic matter down.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: Viking’s numbers became the yardstick for the next landers. When Mars Pathfinder analyzed soil in 1997, its first result came out almost identical to Viking’s; later ones showed more aluminum and magnesium and less iron, sulfur and chlorine. The oxidizing surface changed where to look for organic matter. Radiation and harsh chemicals break it down near the top, so later missions went below. In 2018 the Curiosity rover reported organic molecules in 3-billion-year-old mudstone it had drilled into. Europe’s Rosalind Franklin rover was built with a drill that reaches 2 m, far below the roughly 15 cm of Viking, still the deepest search for organics on Mars.

pages.title: Pioneer Venus 2: four probes at once
pages.summary: Four probes fall through Venus’s clouds at once, and one keeps talking on the ground.

facts.label: Craft
facts.value: Pioneer Venus 2 (the Multiprobe): a bus, one large and three small probes

firsts: With the Pioneer Venus Orbiter, the first study of Venus on a global scale

sections.heading: One craft, five parts
sections.text: Pioneer Venus 2, also called the Multiprobe, was launched on an Atlas-Centaur from Cape Canaveral on 8 August 1978. NASA’s Ames Research Center ran the mission, and Hughes Aircraft built the craft: a drum-shaped bus carrying four probes. The large probe, 1.5 m across, had a parachute; the three identical small probes had none. Each kept its instruments inside a sealed titanium sphere. On 16 November, about 11 million km from Venus, the bus released the large probe. Four days later it spun off the small ones, named for where they were going: the North Probe, the Day Probe and the Night Probe.

sections.heading: Four ways down
sections.text: All four probes entered the atmosphere on 9 December 1978, within minutes of one another, at sites thousands of kilometers apart. The large probe went in on the day side near the equator, shed its heat shield, rode its parachute down to about 45 km, then fell free. The small probes fell all the way on their heat shields alone. The North Probe and the Night Probe went down on the night side, the Day Probe into the southern day side. Each took about an hour to reach the ground. None was built to survive the landing, yet the Day Probe sent data from the surface for 67 minutes, until its batteries ran down.

sections.heading: What they found
sections.text: The probes measured the clouds layer by layer. The main deck lay between about 47 and 70 km up, in three distinct layers made largely of sulfuric acid, and looked much the same at all four sites. Below a thin haze near 30 km the air was clear. Between about 10 and 50 km there was almost no convection, and below 50 km the four probes read nearly the same temperatures. Tracked by radio from Earth, they drifted west with winds that grew from a few meters per second near the ground to about 150 m/s at the cloud tops. And the air held several hundred times more primordial argon and neon than Earth’s.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: The four probes gave a profile of Venus’s air at four places on the same day, from high above the clouds to the ground. Scientists combined their readings with those of the Pioneer Venus Orbiter and the Venera 10, 12 and 13 landers into models of the atmosphere from the surface to 100 km, published in 1985 as the Venus International Reference Atmosphere. NASA’s engineering model of Venus’s air, Venus-GRAM, is built on it and is used to simulate the entry, descent and landing of new craft. In June 1985 the Soviet Vega balloons drifted through the middle cloud layer the probes had charted, and Pioneer Venus probe scientists from Ames helped report what they found.

pages.title: Pioneer 11: the first to Saturn
pages.summary: A backup craft skims Jupiter, then scouts Saturn's rings for the Voyagers.
firsts: First spacecraft to fly past Saturn
First pictures of Jupiter's polar regions

sections.heading: The backup goes closer
sections.text: Pioneer 11 was built as the twin and backup of Pioneer 10. It was launched on an Atlas-Centaur on the evening of 5 April 1973, Florida time. Once Pioneer 10 had survived Jupiter's radiation, the team aimed its sister much closer, about 43,000 km above the cloud tops, less than a third of Pioneer 10's distance. On 3 December 1974 (UT) it swept past at more than 170,000 km/h, climbing steeply from south to north through the worst of the radiation. It returned the best pictures yet of the Great Red Spot and the first ever of Jupiter's poles.

sections.heading: Across the solar system
sections.text: The close pass was also a slingshot. Jupiter's gravity flung Pioneer 11 back across the solar system toward Saturn, some 2.4 billion km away, on a long loop high above the plane in which the planets orbit. The crossing took nearly five years. After Jupiter the craft was officially renamed Pioneer Saturn, though most people kept calling it Pioneer 11. From its high vantage point it also measured the Sun's magnetic field and found it simpler than expected: a northern half and a southern half, divided by a warped sheet that sweeps up and down as the Sun turns.

sections.heading: Through the ring plane
sections.text: By the time Pioneer 11 neared Saturn, Voyager 1 and 2 were on their way there too. NASA had to choose its path: a riskier run inside the rings, which most of the mission's scientists wanted, or one just outside them, the route Voyager 2 would have to take to swing on toward Uranus. NASA chose the outside route, making Pioneer the scout. On 1 September 1979 at 14:36 UT, it crossed the ring plane about 35,000 km beyond the bright rings. Nobody knew whether unseen ring particles would wreck it. The answer took 86 minutes to reach Earth: it had come through.

sections.heading: What it found
sections.text: Pioneer 11 passed about 21,000 km above Saturn's clouds and sent back 440 images of the planet and its moons. They showed a narrow new ring just outside the bright A ring, now called the F ring, and a small moon nobody had seen before. Its particle detectors hinted at more. It found that Saturn gives off more heat than it gets from the Sun, and that its magnetic field lines up almost exactly with its spin axis, unlike Earth's or Jupiter's. The next day it passed Titan, an orange, cloud-wrapped ball, and then headed out of the solar system.

pages.title: Venera 15 and 16: radar maps of Venus
pages.summary: Two orbiters look through Venus’s clouds by radar and map its northern lands.

facts.label: Mapped
facts.value: North of about 30° N, a quarter of Venus

firsts: First detailed radar images of Venus’s surface from orbit

sections.heading: The flight
sections.text: Venera 15 and Venera 16 left Baikonur five days apart, on 2 and 7 June 1983, each on a Proton rocket. They were built on the design of the earlier Veneras, but where a lander had been they carried a large radar antenna, with bigger solar panels to power it. They went into orbit around Venus on 10 and 14 October 1983. Each orbit was a long loop that took about a day, passed over the north pole and swung down to under 1,000 km above the planet, then out to about 65,000 km.

sections.heading: Seeing through clouds
sections.text: Venus is covered by clouds that no camera can see through, but radio waves pass through them. Each orbiter’s radar looked down and to one side as it swept low over the north, building up a long strip of surface image on every pass. A second radar measured the height of the ground below, so the strips could be turned into maps of mountains and plains. Venera 16 usually followed its twin over the same area a few days later. The pictures showed features about 1 to 2 km across, as sharp as the best Earth-based radar.

sections.heading: The northern map
sections.text: Mapping began in October 1983, and the main survey ended on 10 July 1984. By then the two craft had covered Venus from the north pole down to about 30 degrees north, some 115 million square kilometers, about a quarter of the planet. That was ground the giant Arecibo radar on Earth could hardly see. Soviet teams assembled the strips into 27 large mosaics. They showed mountains such as Maxwell Montes, lava plains and impact craters, as well as ringed features later called coronae and crumpled, tile-like ground the Soviet scientists called parquet.

sections.heading: Why it mattered
sections.text: The American Pioneer Venus orbiter had measured the heights of Venus’s surface from 1978 onward, but its radar saw only coarse detail. Venera 15 and 16 gave the first sharp pictures of a large part of the planet, and scientists began to see Venus as a world shaped by volcanoes and buckled crust. In the early 1990s NASA’s Magellan mapped almost all of Venus in far finer detail and confirmed that small hills seen in the Venera images were volcanoes. Venera 15 fell silent in January 1985, and Venera 16 was lost that June.

pages.title: Voyager 1: the Pale Blue Dot
pages.summary: Voyager 1 looks back from 6 billion km, and the Earth is less than a pixel of light.
firsts: First portrait of the solar system from outside

sections.heading: The family portrait
sections.text: By 1990 Voyager 1 had passed Jupiter and Saturn and was heading out of the solar system, with no more worlds to fly by. Its cameras were to be switched off to save power for the long journey. Carl Sagan, a member of the Voyager imaging team, had proposed one last use for them: turn around and photograph the planets from outside. Earlier in the mission the Sun had been too close and bright to point the cameras near it safely. On 14 February 1990 Voyager 1 took a series of frames covering the Sun and six of its planets, a family portrait of the solar system. They were its last pictures.

sections.heading: How far
sections.text: When it took the portrait, Voyager 1 was about 6 billion km from home, roughly 40 times as far from the Sun as the Earth is, and well above the plane in which the planets travel, about 32 degrees. Light from the Sun needed more than five hours to reach it. It had been traveling for more than twelve years, since its launch on 5 September 1977, and had flown past Saturn on 12 November 1980. From there the inner planets sat only a few degrees from the Sun, so close to its glare that the pictures could not be taken earlier.

sections.heading: Less than a pixel
sections.text: In the frame that holds the Earth, taken with the narrow-angle camera through violet, blue and green filters, the whole planet covers about an eighth of a single pixel. It shows as a faint, bluish point of light. By chance it sits inside one of the bands of scattered sunlight that cross the frame, reflections inside the camera from pointing it so near the Sun. Jupiter and Saturn, much larger, filled at least a full pixel in their frames. For the picture's 30th anniversary in 2020, JPL processed the original data again with modern software, trying to stay true to what the planners intended.

sections.heading: Sagan's idea
sections.text: Sagan built his 1994 book, Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space, around this picture. The idea he drew from it is easy to state. Everything people have ever done has happened on that one faint point, and from far enough away our borders, rivalries and sense of importance shrink to nothing. What remains is a small world that all of us share. For Sagan the picture argued for humility, and for taking better care of the Earth and of each other, because nothing within reach could take its place. The voice on this page is Sagan's own, explaining what the picture meant to him.
